procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 22, 1965 of the Punjab High Court in Civil Writ No. 719 of 1964, dismissing the writ petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A learned Single Judge referred the writ petition to a Division Bench. The Division Bench held that the allegation of mala fides had not been proved and that the Additional District Magistrate was competent to make the requisitioning order. Consequently, the writ petition was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed by special leave from the judgment of the Punjab High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal with costs, quashing the impugned order and allowing the writ petition filed in the High Court.

directions: The writ petition filed in the High Court succeeds.
The impugned order shall stand quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Additional District Magistrate, empowered under s. 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to exercise the powers of a District Magistrate, is competent to exercise the powers under s. 29 of the Defence of India Act, 1962, which were specifically delegated by the Central Government to District Magistrates.

facts: The Central Government, under the Defence of India Act, 1962, delegated its power to requisition property (s. 29) to specific officers, including "District Magistrates".

An Additional District Magistrate (ADM) in Punjab, who had been invested with all the powers of a District Magistrate under s. 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, issued an order to requisition a shop.
The validity of this order was challenged on the grounds that the ADM was not the "District Magistrate" to whom the power was specifically delegated.
law: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a District Magistrate (DM) and an Additional District Magistrate (ADM) are two distinct and different authorities. An ADM is subordinate to the DM and does not attain the status of a DM, even if invested with all of the DM's powers.
The powers of requisitioning under the Defence of India Act are of a very drastic and extraordinary nature, affecting fundamental rights to property.

When such drastic powers are delegated, it is presumed that the delegating authority (the Central Government) carefully considered the fitness and high status of the delegate to ensure the power is exercised with responsibility and circumspection.
The words used in a delegation notification, such as "District Magistrate," must be given their plain and normal meaning unless the context requires otherwise.
application: The Court reasoned that because the requisitioning powers were so drastic, the Central Government intentionally delegated them to an officer of the high status and experience of a District Magistrate, who is the head of the executive in the district.
The Court held that the delegation was made to the officer actually holding the office of the District Magistrate, not to anyone who might simply be empowered to exercise a DM's powers.
Empowering an ADM with the powers of a DM under the general Code of Criminal Procedure does not equate them to the specific delegate named in the notification under the special Defence of India Act.

The Court found no reason to deviate from the normal rule of interpretation. Therefore, the specific words "District Magistrate" in the delegation notification could not be read to include an "Additional District Magistrate," as they are legally distinct and separate offices.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the Additional District Magistrate was competent to exercise the delegated power. It held that the power under s. 29 of the Defence of India Act was specifically delegated to the "District Magistrate," a distinct and higher-ranking officer. An Additional District Magistrate, being a different and subordinate authority, could not exercise this power even if empowered with the general powers of a District Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

issue.issue_text: Whether the allegation of mala fides against the requisitioning authority was proved.

facts: The appellant challenged a requisitioning order in the High Court on two grounds.
The first ground was that the order had been made 'mala fide' (in bad faith).
application: The Division Bench of the High Court considered this allegation.
The High Court held that the allegation of 'mala fides' had not been proved.
When the case was appealed to the Supreme Court, the appeal focused on a different issue.
The text states that the 'sole question involved' in the Supreme Court appeal was whether the Additional District Magistrate had the legal authority to issue the requisitioning order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue of mala fides. The text indicates that the High Court had already rejected this allegation, and the appeal to the Supreme Court was based solely on the separate legal question of the Additional District Magistrate's authority.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Additional District Magistrate, empowered under s. 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to exercise the powers of a District Magistrate, is competent to exercise the powers under s. 29 of the Defence of India Act, 1962, which were specifically delegated by the Central Government to District Magistrates.
appellant_arguments: The delegation of power by the Central Government was specifically to the "District Magistrate," and this term cannot be interpreted to include an Additional District Magistrate.

An Additional District Magistrate is of a lower rank than a District Magistrate and is not the same office; only a person appointed under s. 10(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be called a District Magistrate.
The words in the government notification must be read literally, and "District Magistrate" cannot be read as "Additional District Magistrate."

The power given to an Additional District Magistrate under s. 10(2) of the Code to exercise powers under "any other law" does not extend to powers delegated via an executive order, which is distinct from a legislative enactment.
The precedent in the Central Talkies' case is distinguishable because, in that case, the relevant Act allowed the District Magistrate to authorize other officers, which is not the case here.
respondent_arguments: An Additional District Magistrate, when invested by the State Government with the powers of a District Magistrate under s. 10(2) of the Code, squarely falls within the expression "District Magistrate" used in the delegation notification.
The Central Government's intent was to delegate its power to officers who were in fact and actually discharging the duties and functions of a District Magistrate.
The delegation was not meant to be confined only to officers formally appointed as District Magistrates under s. 10(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the allegation of mala fides against the requisitioning authority was proved.
appellant_arguments: The appellant made assertions and contentions alleging that the requisitioning order was issued with mala fide intent.
respondent_arguments: The respondents resisted the petition and controverted the appellant's assertions, denying any mala fides.

cases.case_name: Ajaib Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Unless a person has been appointed under s. 10(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, he cannot be called a District Magistrate, and an Additional District Magistrate is below the rank of a District Magistrate.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statute confers power specifically upon a "District Magistrate," the term must be interpreted literally and does not include an "Additional District Magistrate," even if the latter has been empowered under Section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to exercise all the powers of a District Magistrate. An Additional District Magistrate is of a rank below that of a District Magistrate, and a general empowerment under the Code cannot override the specific designation in another statute.
obiter: The decision is not based on the line of argument of persona designata.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A specific delegation of power by the Central Government to a "District Magistrate" under the Defence of India Act must be interpreted literally and does not extend to an Additional District Magistrate. Even if an Additional District Magistrate is empowered under s. 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to exercise the powers of a District Magistrate under any other law, this does not make them competent to exercise a power specifically and exclusively delegated to the office of the District Magistrate via a separate executive notification.
legal_tests_applied: The normal rule of interpretation that expressions or words used in a notification must be read as such and not in any other manner, unless the context requires otherwise.
why_appellant_lost: The allegation of mala fides was not proved in the High Court, and the Supreme Court did not overturn this finding of fact.
why_respondent_won: The allegation of mala fides against the respondents was not proved by the appellant.
policy_considerations: The powers of requisitioning are of a very drastic nature and involve fundamental rights to property. Therefore, the Central Government, when delegating such power, must be presumed to have been fully conscious of this and intentionally empowered only an officer of the high status of a District Magistrate to exercise it.
